slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter seven: the examination of the conditioned.

slides.heading: Things begin, last and end
points: A cup is made, lasts, and one day breaks
Three marks: arising, abiding, ceasing
What could be more obvious?
slides.say: Everything around us seems to have a life story. A cup is made, it lasts for some years, and one day it breaks. A thought comes up, stays for a moment and is gone. Buddhist teachers of Nagarjuna's time put this into a formula: whatever is conditioned has three marks, arising, abiding and ceasing. It is one of the most trusted descriptions in the tradition. Things begin, they last, they end. What could be more obvious?

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: The longest chapter so far
Each mark looked for in turn: none is found
Ends with a dream, a magic show, a city in the clouds
slides.say: This chapter, the longest so far, tests that formula. If arising, abiding and ceasing are real features that things have from their own side, we should be able to find them, say what they are and say when they happen. Nagarjuna looks, one mark at a time, and none of them is found. At the end he says what they are like instead: a dream, a magic show, a city in the clouds.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
Thirty-four verses
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: The three marks as forces
points: Arising, abiding, ceasing: real factors
One brings a thing into being, one holds it, one ends it
Is arising itself conditioned or not?
slides.say: Now the explanation. The Abhidharma schools held that every conditioned thing carries three marks: it arises, it abides and it ceases. The marks were not just ways of talking. They were counted as real factors in their own right, little forces that act on a thing: one brings it into being, one holds it in being for a moment, one takes it out of being. Nagarjuna starts with a simple question about the marks themselves, in verse seven point one. Is arising conditioned or unconditioned?

slides.heading: Is arising conditioned?
slides.say: Suppose arising is conditioned. Then every conditioned thing has the three marks, so arising must itself arise, abide and cease, and its arising must arise in turn, without end. Before the cup can arise, the arising of the cup must arise, and before that, the arising of that arising. Suppose instead arising is unconditioned, like space in the Abhidharma list. Then how can it be the mark of things that come and go? A mark of change that never changes is a strange mark. And do the three marks act one at a time or together? One at a time, none is enough. All together, they clash: nothing can be arising and ceasing in the same instant.

slides.heading: Arising that produces itself
slides.say: The Abhidharma had an answer to the regress. There are only two arisings, they said. The primary arising produces the thing and also a secondary arising, and the secondary arising in turn produces the primary one. Each produces the other, so the chain closes into a loop of two. Nagarjuna asks about the order. For the secondary to produce the primary, it must already exist. But it exists only because the primary produced it. Each needs the other to be already there before it can be there itself. And could one produce the other while still being produced? Only if something not yet born could do things. A builder who has not yet been born cannot build a house.

slides.heading: The lamp that lights itself
slides.say: The opponent reaches for a famous image. A lamp lights up the room, and it lights up itself too. In the same way, arising could produce both the thing and itself. Nagarjuna looks closely. To light something up is to remove darkness from it. Is there darkness inside the flame? No. In the spot where the flame stands? No. So the lamp lighting itself describes nothing. And the darkness around it? While the lamp is catching, its light and the darkness never meet: where there is light there is no darkness. If the lamp could remove darkness without reaching it, a lamp lit here would remove the darkness of every room in the world. And if light lights itself, darkness should hide itself, and we could not even see that it is dark. None of this stops anyone reading by lamplight. What fails is the idea of a lamp with a power of its own, crossing over to act on a separate thing called darkness.

slides.heading: The three-part test
slides.say: Nagarjuna now asks directly whether arising can produce itself. If it has not yet arisen, it is not there to do anything. If it has already arisen, there is nothing left to produce. Then he brings in the pattern of chapter two. There, the road was split into the part walked, the part not yet walked and the part being walked. Here the same split is made for arising. What has already arisen does not arise again; what has not arisen is not there to arise; and what is arising is not a third, half-born thing between the two. The diagram shows the same test applied to all three marks, nine boxes in all. In none of them is a mark found doing its work.

slides.heading: At peace as regards own-nature
points: Arising is not found apart from the arising thing
Whatever comes to be in dependence is at peace
Because things depend, they are free of the marks
slides.say: Verses fifteen and sixteen are compressed, and commentators unpack them differently. The thread is this. Arising has not been found as anything separate from the arising thing, so we cannot say the thing arises in dependence on an arising, as if there were two items. And here Nagarjuna gives one of the most important statements in the text: whatever comes to be in dependence is, as regards own nature, at peace. At peace means quiet, empty of own nature, not stirred by an arising of its own. Because things depend, they are free of the three marks taken as real forces. The next verses tie up the other options: there is no unarisen thing waiting to arise, and arising fits neither what exists nor what does not.

slides.heading: Abiding: does anything stay?
points: What abides need not abide again
Every thing is always ageing
No pause between arising and ceasing
slides.say: The middle mark is abiding, a thing's staying in being for a while. It is the mark we rely on most. The same test: a thing not abiding does not abide; a thing already abiding does not need to abide again; a thing in the act of abiding is not a third case. Then a point anyone can check. Every thing is always ageing. There is no stretch of time, however short, in which a cup is simply staying the same, untouched by the wear that will one day break it. Which thing ever stands still, outside ageing and death? None is found. So abiding is not a separate state, a pause between arising and ceasing.

slides.heading: Ceasing: does anything end?
points: What has not ceased is still there
What has ceased does not cease again
You cannot cut off a second head
slides.say: The last mark is ceasing. Surely things end: the cup breaks, the candle goes out. The test again. What has not ceased is still there, intact. What has ceased does not cease again. What is ceasing is not a third, half-gone thing. A state cannot cease while it is still that state, and it cannot cease when it is already a different state. The edge where one becomes the other is not found as a thing in its own right. Two short images close the case. A thing that exists cannot cease while it exists. And a thing that does not exist cannot cease, just as you cannot cut off a second head that someone does not have.

slides.heading: Conditioned and unconditioned
slides.say: The chapter draws its conclusion in verse thirty-three. If arising, abiding and ceasing are not established as real marks, then the conditioned, defined by those marks, is not established either. And then a step that surprised Nagarjuna's opponents: if the conditioned is not established, neither is the unconditioned. Nirvana and space were defined as what has no arising, abiding or ceasing. Take away one side of the contrast, and the other side has nothing to stand on. So nirvana is not a second, better realm standing on its own beyond the world of change. Chapter twenty-five returns to this.

slides.heading: A dream, a magic show
points: Like a dream, a magic show, a city in the clouds
Vivid, with effects, and not found on waking
Not that nothing happens
slides.say: The last verse does not deny the life story of things. It describes it. Arising, abiding and ceasing are like a magic show, like a dream, like a city of gandharvas: the towers that seem to stand in the clouds and are not found when you walk towards them. In a dream, a house is built, stands and burns down. These events are vivid, they follow their own logic, and they move the dreamer to joy and fear. Yet none of them is found anywhere on waking. So the verse does not say that nothing happens. It says that what happens, happens the way a dream happens: fully, vividly, with effects, and without anything that arises, lasts or ends from its own side.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: A cup is still made, used and broken
The marks work as designations
Not a frozen world
slides.say: A cup is still made in a pottery, used for years and dropped on a kitchen floor. We can still say when it was made and when it broke, and we are right. Doctors still date the onset of an illness. What the chapter removes is the idea that arising, abiding and ceasing are real forces or stages a thing passes through on its own: a moment when being switches on, a stretch when it holds steady, a moment when it switches off. The three marks work as designations within before and after. And the world is not frozen. A frozen world would need things that truly abide, and abiding was not found either. The world as it appears, changing, workable and dream-like, is exactly what is left.

points: Substrateless World: Chapters 3 and 8
The Logic of Dependency (bonus article)
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World: chapter three, on non-arising and the question does this moment arise or cease, and chapter eight, on dreaming. The bonus article, The Logic of Dependency, on change without a changer. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter eight, the examination of the agent and action.
